red.focus: Find law before relying on it
red.summary: Legal research is the process of finding the rules and decisions that actually govern a problem. Learn to distinguish primary legal authorities from explanations and commentary.
checklist: I can identify primary and secondary legal sources
I can locate a governing statute or decision
I can check source jurisdiction and date

sections.title: Start With a Precise Question
sections.body_md: A client asks whether a landlord may keep a security deposit. First identify the place, type of tenancy, relevant dates, and what the deposit covered. Those details determine which law might govern. Then search statutes, regulations and relevant decisions rather than beginning with a general website about rental disputes. Legal research begins by turning a human question into identifiable legal issues. That approach saves time and avoids gathering dozens of unrelated documents that cannot answer the client.

sections.title: Primary Law and Helpful Explanations
sections.body_md: A statute, regulation, constitutional provision or court judgment can be a primary legal source. A textbook, practice guide or article may explain those authorities and help find them, but it is generally a secondary source. A good researcher uses secondary material to understand the field, then verifies the rule in relevant primary law. Copying a textbook sentence without checking whether the statute has changed can leave the client with outdated advice.

sections.title: Jurisdiction and Date Matter
sections.body_md: A case from another country may be insightful but not binding. A statute may have been amended since the event at issue. A court judgment may have been reversed. For every source record its jurisdiction, authority, effective date, citation and current status. These small habits make later writing easier because the evidence supporting the rule is visible. The researcher should never promise that a rule applies until the source has been checked against the client's location and timeline.

yellow.focus: Verify that a legal source remains controlling
yellow.summary: Learn how to follow a rule from an initial search to its current authoritative form. Distinguish an amendment, repeal, overruling, and a later decision that merely distinguishes the source.
checklist: I can check subsequent judicial treatment
I can verify statutory versions at relevant dates
I can trace a proposition to authoritative text

sections.title: A Search Result Is Only the Beginning
sections.body_md: Suppose a case appears to support a tenant's right to a refund. Before citing it, confirm that the decision comes from a court with the relevant authority, that its holding actually addresses the issue, and that later cases have not limited it. Citation services may flag negative treatment, but a flag does not explain what changed. Read the later decision and determine whether it overruled, distinguished or simply criticized the earlier reasoning.

sections.title: Statutes Have Histories
sections.body_md: A provision found in today's code may not have been in force when the client's events occurred. Amendments can change definitions, exceptions or remedies, and transitional provisions may determine which version applies. A careful researcher records the enactment, amendment history, commencement dates and any relevant saving clause. When the client is accused of conduct from several years ago, using only the present text can produce a serious legal error. The time dimension is as important as geography.

sections.title: Build a Verifiable Source Trail
sections.body_md: A sound memorandum allows another lawyer to reconstruct its central legal proposition. Record the precise statutory section or passage in the judgment, the court, date and reason for relevance. Link the secondary explanation to the primary source it describes. Avoid treating an AI-generated citation or unattributed quotation as real until independently verified. Good legal writing does not simply look well sourced; it makes the source trail inspectable by people whose decisions depend on it.

orange.summary: Develop a research strategy for issues with overlapping statutes, multiple courts and uncertain doctrine. Evaluate adverse sources and avoid turning the longest research result into the apparent rule.
checklist: I can build a hierarchy-aware research plan
I can synthesize holdings with clear factual limits

sections.title: Plan the Research Before Opening Tabs
sections.body_md: For a cross-border commercial dispute, list jurisdiction, forum, governing-law clauses, issues and likely primary sources. Separate controlling materials from persuasive comparisons. Begin with the most authoritative source that might resolve each question, then follow cited statutes, cases and regulations to their current versions. An organized plan prevents endless browsing and helps explain why the researcher stopped. It also makes the research reproducible when another lawyer reviews or updates the work.

sections.title: Synthesis Needs a Narrow Rule
sections.body_md: Several decisions may address similar claims with different facts and procedural postures. Summarizing each separately is not enough. Identify the common legal principle, the distinction each court treated as important, and the unanswered question. Do not stitch quotations together to manufacture a test no court actually adopted. An accurate synthesis shows both the best-supported proposition and the boundaries of its authority. The reader should be able to trace each step without guessing.

sections.title: Record the Negative Case
sections.body_md: A lawyer who finds three favorable decisions but omits one controlling adverse decision has produced unreliable research. Adverse authority may be distinguishable, limited or overridden, but it must be examined. State its strongest effect on the proposed conclusion and explain the response supported by law. Where the issue is genuinely unsettled, distinguish possible outcomes and identify what factual or legal development could change the advice. Research excellence is measured by reliable understanding, not citation volume.

black.focus: Design research methods for contested and transnational sources
black.summary: At doctoral depth, treat legal research as an epistemic discipline shaped by institutional power, language and access. Develop an audit trail that supports both academic critique and practical responsibility.
checklist: I can critique systematic omissions from legal databases
I can develop a reproducible transnational source protocol
I can distinguish authentic sources from misleading or fabricated citations

sections.title: The Database Is Not the Whole Law
sections.body_md: Digitized opinions can privilege higher courts, dominant languages and recent published disputes. Legal practices of communities without extensive formal reporting may be underrepresented. A doctoral legal researcher must identify these selection effects before making general claims about a jurisdiction. Supplement reported cases with statutes, official gazettes, institutional records, scholarship and, when justified, properly conducted empirical inquiry. Absence from a searchable database is not proof that a legal practice does not exist.

sections.title: Translation Can Change the Rule
sections.body_md: A transnational study may compare terms such as good faith, equity, public order or customary law. Their linguistic similarities may conceal different legal tests and histories. A defensible method records the source language, translator, official status and context. It distinguishes an authoritative translation from an explanatory paraphrase, especially when liability depends on a technical term. Intellectual honesty requires admitting when linguistic uncertainty prevents a reliable conclusion and seeking qualified assistance rather than presenting a convenient English rendering as exact.

sections.title: An Audit-Ready Research Record
sections.body_md: A rigorous research report should document the question, search strategy, sources consulted, exclusions, subsequent-treatment checks, date of review and remaining uncertainty. It should distinguish verified quotations from interpretive summaries and disclose the use and verification of automated tools. This is not bureaucratic decoration. It protects clients and scholarly readers from hidden mistakes, fabricated authority and selective evidence. A great lawyer makes conclusions independently examinable because coercive legal decisions deserve more than confidence.
